title: Hidden by the seasons
summary: Arctic Alaska swings about 30 °C between winter and summer every year. Remove that cycle and a steady warming appears.

steps.message: Setting up the investigation you chose...
Plan (structured): Chosen directly: Temperature at 2 Meters over Arctic Alaska North Slope, 1981-2025.
Querying NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources) for Temperature at 2 Meters (T2M) over Arctic Alaska North Slope, 1981-2025...
Averaged 144 grid cells over Arctic Alaska North Slope (weighted by area) into 540 monthly values. Source: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources).
Checking temporal coverage, gaps, and outliers...
Data quality OK — 100% complete, 45.0 years, 0 outliers flagged.
Building monthly means, removing the seasonal cycle, and calculating the trend...
Temperature at 2 Meters is increasing at +0.5469 degC per decade (Sen's slope on 45 annual means). Found 3 change point(s).

trend.basis_reason: Some months vary far more than others here (for example a wet season and a dry season), so pooling monthly values would let the quiet months hide the trend. Annual means were tested instead.

finding.interpretation: Temperature at 2 m over the Arctic Alaska North Slope rose by about 0.55 °C per decade between 1981 and 2025, a statistically significant trend (p = 3.3 × 10⁻⁵) with a 95 % confidence interval of 0.032–0.076 °C yr⁻¹ and a total increase of ~2.4 °C. The warming is spatially coherent, with 98.6 % of grid cells showing significant increases, and is most pronounced in the summer (JJA) and autumn (SON) seasons, which both reach statistical significance. The effect size (≈2.6 × the inter‑annual variability) indicates that the observed change is large relative to natural fluctuations, suggesting scientific relevance beyond mere statistical significance.
finding.limitations: A documented step change in 1993 (+1.52 °C) may inflate the apparent monotonic trend, and the linear model does not capture such abrupt shifts. Winter and spring trends are not statistically significant, highlighting seasonal variability in the signal. The analysis assumes data completeness and uniform quality across the 45‑year record, which may not fully hold.

provenance.source_name: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources)
provenance.processing_method: Monthly NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources) values on 144 grid cells averaged over the region with cos(latitude) area weights (a month counts only when at least 70% of the region's area has data), aggregated to annual means, then trend-tested.
provenance.statistical_method: Sen's slope with a Mann-Kendall test on annual means, both corrected for lag-1 autocorrelation (r1 = 0.02); OLS t-test with effective sample size n_eff = 43 as a second check

concern_reasons: Statistically clear and large next to normal swings (effect size 2.63).
A change in this direction is generally harmful for this variable.
confidence_reasons: The trend held up in both halves of the record, with caveats (for example an abrupt step).
The skeptic review found it held up, with objections worth keeping in mind.

insight.headline: Sustained warming raises heat stress and speeds up melting and drying.

evidence.text: 3 abrupt steps were detected (1993, 2016, 2020), so a single steady trend is a poor description of this record. Repeated steps often reflect regime changes or data-source discontinuities rather than gradual driving.
The underlying data is reanalysis (model-assimilated) averaged over the region's grid cells, so a trend can partly reflect changes in the observing system rather than the climate.

drivers.title: Greenhouse-gas warming
drivers.text: Rising CO₂ and other greenhouse gases are the dominant cause of the global warming trend measured since the mid-20th century.

drivers.title: Local land use and urban heat
drivers.text: Land clearing, changes in irrigation and growing cities can add local warming on top of the global signal.

drivers.title: Natural variability
drivers.text: El Niño/La Niña and multi-decade ocean cycles can push a regional record up or down for years at a time.

impacts.text: More dangerous heat days raise the risk of heat illness, especially for outdoor workers, older people and homes without cooling.
Heat during flowering and grain-filling can cut yields, and warmer nights raise crop water demand.
Higher evaporation dries soils and shrinks reservoirs faster.
Species ranges shift, and heat plus drought raise wildfire and forest stress.
Cooling demand and peak electricity load rise.

mitigate: Cut fossil-fuel emissions: renewables, efficiency, electrified transport and heating.
Protect and restore forests, peatlands and wetlands that store carbon.
Reduce methane from leaks, landfills and livestock, which acts quickly on warming.
Global action — one region cannot reverse a global trend, but it can cut its own share.
adapt: Heat-health action plans and early-warning systems.
Urban trees, cool roofs and shaded public space.
Heat-tolerant crop varieties and shifted planting dates.
Efficient irrigation and a power grid built for peak cooling load.
insight.region_context: Permafrost tundra in a part of the world that is warming faster than the global average.
